new.definition: A rich soup of turtle meat chopped fine and simmered in stock, a classic of New Orleans Creole cooking. Brennan's published recipe finishes it with chopped hard-boiled egg, fresh spinach, lemon and sherry. The egg adds richness and the sherry a dry, nutty lift. Mock turtle soup, its English cousin, carries no turtle at all: it was made from calf's head.
new.guest: Our Turtle Soup is a New Orleans Creole classic: turtle meat simmered into a rich, savory soup, with brown butter spinach and grated egg through it and a splash of aged Sherry to finish. If you have never had turtle, think of a deep, finely chopped stew.
new.kitchen: The everyday menu prints 100% turtle meat, brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged Sherry. It carries alcohol, egg and butter; ask the kitchen what thickens it before answering any question about flour or gluten.
new.compare: Mock turtle soup is the English imitation, made from calf's head with no turtle in it; a Creole turtle soup is made from turtle meat, and ours prints all turtle.

new.background: Turtle soup was a dish of the elite in eighteenth century England, made from green turtles brought in by ship, and its cost gave rise to mock turtle soup, made from calf's head for those who could not afford the real thing. Hannah Glasse (1708 to 1770) printed a recipe for dressing a turtle the West India way in her Art of Cookery. In America cooks made it from native turtles such as the snapping turtle and the terrapin, and New Orleans took it into its Creole cooking. The Picayune's Creole Cook Book of 1901 prints a green turtle soup, a second turtle soup and a recipe for mock eggs for turtle soup. Brennan's own published recipe carries the egg forward, chopped hard-boiled, with sherry, fresh spinach and lemon.
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Classic Turtle Soup

new.definition: A large freshwater turtle of North America, long cooked into American turtle soup. Two kinds share the name: the common snapping turtle, found from southern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, and the alligator snapping turtle, the largest freshwater turtle in the United States, with three rows of large, pronounced ridges down its shell. The alligator snapper alone carries a worm-like lure on its tongue, which it wriggles to draw fish into reach.
new.guest: The turtle in our soup is Louisiana freshwater turtle, not sea turtle. It is cooked down and chopped fine, so it eats like a rich, savory stew, and it is never the turtles you may have seen in our courtyard.
new.kitchen: Which snapper the kitchen buys, and from whom, is the chef's to say. Never name a species, a farm or a supplier until lineup confirms it.
new.compare: The alligator snapper has three rows of large, pronounced ridges down its shell and a lure on its tongue; the common snapper's shell is lower and smoother, and it has no lure.

new.background: Louisiana long traded wild snapping turtles. By 1998 it was the only state that still allowed the commercial harvest of the wild alligator snapping turtle, and the United States Geological Survey calls it the last state to end the practice. Worry over the harvest brought a regulation from the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries, which took effect late in 2004, barring the commercial harvest of the wild alligator snapper and limiting personal take to one a day for each boat or vehicle. The common snapping turtle ranges far more widely, from southern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, and people in many parts of the United States eat it in soups and stews.

new.definition: A fortified wine from the Jerez district of Andalusia, in southern Spain. It ages in a solera, tiers of barrels in which the wine drawn for bottling from the oldest is replaced from the next younger, so every bottle blends many years. The dry styles run from pale fino, aged under a film of yeast called flor, through amontillado, which starts under flor and then ages in contact with air, to darker, richer oloroso. In the kitchen a splash of dry, aged sherry finishes a rich soup.
new.guest: We finish the turtle soup with a splash of aged Sherry, the fortified wine of Jerez in southern Spain. Its dry, nutty taste lifts the richness of the soup, much as a squeeze of lemon lifts a piece of fish.
new.kitchen: Which Sherry finishes the soup, and whether it goes in at the stove or at the table, is a lineup question. Tell any guest avoiding alcohol that it is in the soup, and never promise that it cooks off.
new.compare: Fino and manzanilla age under flor and stay pale; amontillado begins under flor and then ages with air; oloroso ages with air and is darker and richer. The menu prints aged Sherry, not which style.

new.background: Sherry takes its name from Jerez de la Frontera, which with Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María makes the sherry triangle of Cádiz. English drinkers knew it as sack, and in 1587 Francis Drake (about 1540 to 1596) raided Cádiz and carried off close to three thousand casks of it. William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) gave Falstaff a speech in praise of sherris sack in Henry IV, Part 2. In 1933 Spain's first wine statute recognized the denominación de origen Jerez, and in 1935 its Consejo Regulador, the first in Spain, was set up to keep its rules. In the Creole kitchen sherry is a finish: Brennan's published turtle soup recipe adds it with the egg, spinach and lemon at the end.
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Classic Turtle Soup, finished with aged Sherry

new.definition: A tender leafy green, eaten raw in salads or cooked. Heat collapses it fast: a heaped pan wilts to a few spoonfuls in a minute, so cooks squeeze it hard before it joins a cream or a gratin. Its flavor is mineral and faintly bitter, which is why butter, cream and garlic suit it.
new.guest: Our turtle soup carries brown butter spinach, spinach cooked with butter taken to a nutty brown, all through the bowl. On the Thanksgiving menu the Rockefeller Gratin baked creamed spinach with oysters and bacon under breadcrumbs.
new.kitchen: Wash it well, cook it in seconds and squeeze it dry, or it waters down the dish. Whether the creamed spinach carries stock or cheese is the kitchen's to say for a guest who asks.
new.compare: Swiss chard is used the same way, but its thick stalks need a head start; spinach's leaves and thin stems cook in the same moment.

new.background: Spinach is thought to have been domesticated in ancient Persia, and from there it traveled east to China by the seventh century and west toward Europe. The Moors brought it to Spain, where written record places it by the eleventh century, and from Spain it spread across the continent. French cooks call a dish set on a bed of spinach à la Florentine, a name tradition ties to Catherine de' Medici (1519 to 1589), the Florentine who became queen of France, though the story is legend rather than record. In New Orleans spinach is bound up with oysters: Antoine's, which dates Oysters Rockefeller to 1899, has long said its recipe holds no spinach, yet most cooks since have made it with spinach, as the Thanksgiving Rockefeller Gratin did with creamed spinach.
new.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Classic Turtle Soup (brown butter spinach) and Rockefeller Gratin (creamed spinach)

new.definition: The two Louisiana cooking traditions. Creole is the cooking of New Orleans, its households and restaurants, French at the root and shaped by Spanish, West African and Native American cooks, with butter, cream, tomato and sauces. Cajun is the country cooking of the Acadians, French speaking exiles from Canada who made new homes on the bayous and prairies west of the city, a cooking of one pot, rice, pork, shellfish and game. The two share techniques such as the roux and the trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper.
new.guest: Creole is New Orleans city cooking, French at heart, with butter, cream and tomato; Cajun is the country cooking of the Acadians to the west, built around one pot and rice. Brennan's is a Creole house, and our turtle soup and gumbo are Creole soups.
new.kitchen: A dish's label is the menu's: call it Creole or Cajun only as the menu or the chef does, and leave how hot a dish runs to the kitchen.
new.compare: Creole is the city and Cajun the country: Creole cooking reaches for butter, cream and tomato, Cajun for pork, shellfish and game cooked in one pot over rice.

new.background: Creole comes through French créole and Spanish criollo from a Portuguese word for someone born in the colonies, and in Louisiana it came to name people born there, of any color. Two cookbooks of 1885 carried the city's cooking to a wider audience: La Cuisine Creole, credited to Lafcadio Hearn (1850 to 1904), and The Creole Cookery Book of the Christian Woman's Exchange, a New Orleans women's charity, both published for the World's Industrial and Cotton Centennial Exposition. The Cajuns descend from the Acadians, whom the British began removing from their homeland in 1755; from 1764 exiles reached Louisiana and settled the bayous and prairies west of the city, where many raised cattle. Their cooking reached the whole country after Paul Prudhomme (1940 to 2015), born near Opelousas, opened K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen in the French Quarter in 1979.

deepen.background: A plant wilts when its cells lose the water pressure, called turgor, that holds a leaf firm, and a cook wilts greens on purpose with a short burst of heat from a hot pan, a hot broth or a hot dressing. Appalachian cooks made a spring dish of it, killed lettuce or killed salad, also spelled kilt, in which hot grease is poured over fresh garden lettuce so the leaves just slump. The Dictionary of Smoky Mountain English defines killed salad as a salad made by pouring boiling grease over lettuce or other greens, the same as wilted salad. The same quick heat suits spinach, which takes seconds, and the sturdier collard greens that Brennan's everyday menu of November 2026 set wilted under its Pecan Gulf Fish.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Classic Turtle Soup, its brown butter spinach; on the everyday menu, the wilted collard greens under the Pecan Gulf Fish
deepen.guest: Wilted greens are warmed just until the leaves soften, so they stay tender and bright rather than stewed.
